title: OmniAct: One Policy, One Million Embodiments
summary: A single policy that controls diverse robots must not only transfer task knowledge across embodiments, but also adapt its behavior to each robot's capabilities. Existing approaches facilitate transfer through shared action representations, but these representations do not necessarily capture how differences in robot morphology should shape manipulation strategies. We introduce OmniAct, a cross-embodiment manipulation policy that conditions directly on each robot's kinematics in a specific scene to produce embodiment-specific behavior. This kinematic graph represents the robot's joint positions, motion axes, and connectivity to its visual observation, allowing the policy to account for how its embodiment related to objects and surfaces in the scene. A flow-matching policy predicts relative joint motions for each node, enabling control across robots with different degrees of freedom and kinematic configurations. To learn how physical structure shapes behavior at scale, we procedurally design and filter one million physically feasible robot embodiments; next, we develop algorithms to generate robot trajectories in simulation for all embodiments; finally, we train across diverse simulated manipulation tasks. On 2,000 embodiment-scene-held-out evaluation episodes, OmniAct achieves 63.0% success, compared to 17.8% for pi 0.5 and 57.9% for the strongest baseline; on the task families GPT-6 Astra was evaluated on, it achieves 64.7% against GPT-6 Astra's 41.1%. On a previously unseen real-world robot, it achieves nearly twice the success rate of the next best method, MolmoAct2. Beyond task success, we observe that OmniAct learns distinct manipulation strategies that exploit the capabilities and accommodate the limitations of different morphologies. Project: https://omniact.github.io/

title: DiaCap: Jointly Learning Who Speaks When for Audiovisual Dialogue Captioning
summary: We present DiaCap, an audiovisual LLM for comprehensive dialogue captioning, which produces the transcript, timestamps, and a visual description of the speaker for every utterance in a video. Considering that utterance timing and audiovisual diarization are tightly coupled, DiaCap unifies the tasks in a single model, trained in two complementary stages. First, we train DiaCap on 225K curated clips, using synthetic captions that densely label every utterance in detail. Second, we further refine the model via reinforcement learning on 2.9K human-corrected clips, using fine-grained feedback that directly evaluates utterance timing, speaker grouping, and speaker binding. On DiaDemBench, which we extend with utterance-level timestamps and subtitle redaction, both DiaCap with off-the-shelf transcripts and its end-to-end variant DiaCap-E2E achieve strong results. Specifically, DiaCap performs on par with Gemini 4 Argon in audiovisual diarization while clearly outperforming it in timestamp accuracy (76.59 vs. 42.76 TIME). It also maintains strong diarization on multilingual and minute-long videos, and transfers to audiovisual question answering.

title: BioLoom: Scaling Biomedical Vision-Language Models by Learning from the Structure of Scientific Articles
summary: The development of biomedical vision-language models (VLMs) with contrastive image-text pretraining has been driven by scaling to increasingly large and diverse image-text datasets. Beyond scaling, further progress can come from learning richer representations from existing data. We hypothesize that the structure of scientific literature itself provides an additional source of supervision: figures, panels, captions, and accompanying article text encode rich relationships across modalities. Yet, treating these as independent image-text pairs overlooks their relationships. To address this limitation, we incorporate these structural relationships into contrastive image-text supervision. We preserve exact image-text matches while introducing weaker positive supervision for related pairs, such as a panel and the caption of a sibling panel. We upweight cross-article negatives of the same content type to encourage finer discrimination. We also enrich panel descriptions using visual content, original figure captions, and mentioning paragraphs. Pairing panels with these descriptions and whole figures with their original captions yields Loom52M, a dataset of 52.4 million image-text pairs spanning scientific charts and biomedical images. Using Loom52M, BioLoom (DFN-2B) achieves 56.82% domain-balanced mean accuracy across 67 zero-shot classification tasks from 43 datasets in 10 domains, compared with 48.77% for MedPMC-CLIP. On BioLoomBench with concise captions and BioMedFlickr, it achieves bidirectional mean Recall@1 of 63.20% and 10.59%, versus 46.37% and 7.55% for the respective strongest evaluated baselines, BiomedCLIP and MedPMC-CLIP. Code, datasets, benchmarks, and models are available at https://bioloom-clip.github.io/.

title: CoT-Proxy: Cross-Format Transfer for Distilling Long-Horizon Policies
summary: Reasoning models become long-horizon agents through reinforcement learning or, more cheaply, through fine-tuning on a stronger teacher's trajectories, which contain the teacher's chain-of-thought as well as its actions. The standard fine-tuning approach imitates both, yet the strongest teachers are closed models whose chain-of-thought is hidden behind an API. We show that the chain-of-thought can be left out altogether and that the long-horizon policy can be distilled from the teacher's actions alone. The student is trained on these trajectories with its reasoning block left empty, while a KL loss on a replay buffer of its own generations limits drift from its initial model. Surprisingly, the policy learned from these trajectories with an empty reasoning block carries over to inference with thinking enabled, where the student reasons in its own style while acting like the teacher, an effect we call cross-format transfer. Distilling the actions of Qwen3.6-27B raises the task success of Qwen3-4B on AppWorld from 7% to 18% and that of Qwen3-32B from 12% to 25%. We further introduce CoT-proxies, short summaries of the teacher's reasoning placed after the empty reasoning block, which raise Qwen3-4B further, to 35%. Since neither actions nor CoT-proxies need the hidden chain-of-thought, the recipe applies unchanged to closed teachers. Distilling GPT-5.6 Luna from its visible outputs and the reasoning summaries its API returns raises Qwen3-4B from 7% to 48% on AppWorld and from 3% to 28% on SWE-bench Verified.

title: PyRUA-Dex: Learning Programmatic Policies for Dexterous Bimanual Manipulation with Coding Agents
summary: Learning for dexterous manipulation is limited by the scarcity of high-quality demonstrations: retargeting from human video is imprecise, teleoperation gives no force feedback to the operator, and exoskeleton-based collection is hard to scale up. We present PyRUA-Dex, a framework that enables coding agents to develop dexterous manipulation through programmatic policy, without the need of demonstrations. The programmatic policy is developed in two stages: during exploration, multiple agents explore in parallel for task skills and ways to compose them, and a distilling agent condenses the successful attempts into a task library and one program. During refinement, this program is improved through randomized layouts for enhanced robustness and execution efficiency. In simulated environments, PyRUA-Dex achieves SOTA on Bench2Dex with a score of 72.9 and reaches 81.0% success on DexJoCo under full randomization, ahead of every trained policy on both benchmarks. In real world experiments on a bimanual platform with two 22-DoF hands, PyRUA-Dex learns to play piano, write calligraphy, and other tasks efficiently: learning a new piece from sheet music takes as little as 30 minutes. These results suggest that PyRUA-Dex is an effective framework for developing dexterous manipulation policies with coding agents in the absence of high quality dexterous manipulation demonstrations.

title: Error Direction of Large Language Models on Medical Multiple-Response Questions: Opportunity-Standardized Benchmark Study.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) attain high accuracy on medical examinations, yet evaluations rely predominantly on single-best-answer multiple-choice questions and report only overall accuracy. Multiple-response items, termed X-type in China, require selecting every correct option and remain understudied. Whether models err by omitting correct options or by commissioning incorrect ones has yet to be assessed within an opportunity-standardized framework. This study aimed to quantify the accuracy penalty of multiple-response (X-type) items relative to single-select items and to determine, after standardizing for the unequal numbers of correct and incorrect options, whether LLMs lean toward omission or commission. We analyzed 1644 text-based items from 10 examination cohorts (2017-2026) of the Chinese National Postgraduate Entrance Examination in Clinical Medicine, comprising 1344 single-select items of types A1, A2, A3, and B, and 300 X-type items. Five LLMs, DeepSeek V4 Pro, Kimi K3, Doubao Seed-2.1-pro, GPT-5.6 Sol, and Gemini-3.6 Flash, were tested zero-shot bilingually, yielding 16,440 planned responses. Item-type effects were estimated using generalized estimating equations with cluster-robust standard errors, adjusting for model, language, discipline, and cohort. Opportunity-standardized error direction was analyzed 2 ways: an option-level model treating each option as 1 judgment record and the omission-bias index. Of 16,440 planned responses, 16,426 (99.91%) were evaluable. X-type accuracy (2527/3000, 84.23%) was markedly below single-select accuracy (12,990/13,426, 96.75%; adjusted odds ratio at GPT-5.6 Sol in Chinese 0.17, 95% CI 0.11-0.26; P<.001), a gap of 12.52 percentage points observed and 13.55 adjusted, with no statistically significant item type × model or item type × language interaction (P=.19 and P=.82). Raw counts suggested more strict omissions (245/3000, 8.17%) than overselections (201/3000, 6.70%), but X-type items averaged 2.79 correct vs 1.21 incorrect options per item, a 2.3-fold imbalance in error opportunities. After opportunity standardization, the per-opportunity false-selection rate was 6.69% (242/3620), roughly twice the 3.57% per-opportunity omission rate (299/8380; rate ratio 1.87, 95% CI 1.28-2.74; adjusted odds ratio at the reference model and language 0.38, 95% CI 0.20-0.70; P=.002), so the tilt is modest on the absolute scale and close to 2-fold on the relative scale. Strict omission showed no between-model difference (all Holm-adjusted pairwise comparisons, P≥.46). LLMs incur a substantial accuracy penalty on medical multiple-response items. The apparent omission dominance in raw counts is an artifact of answer-key opportunity imbalance; after opportunity standardization, models show a commission tilt that is modest on the absolute scale (3.12 percentage points per opportunity) and close to 2-fold on the relative scale, and that holds in every model-language condition and in the answer-key stratum whose opportunity base is exactly balanced. Medical LLM benchmarks should report accuracy stratified by item type and error direction on an opportunity-standardized basis.

title: Prediction Models for Frailty in People Living with HIV: Systematic Review.
abstract: Frailty is increasingly prevalent among people living with HIV, who experience earlier onset and a higher burden of frailty than the general population. Prediction models that identify people living with HIV at risk of future frailty could enable timely, targeted intervention. However, the evidence on prediction models developed specifically for frailty in people living with HIV has not yet been systematically evaluated. This review aims to systematically identify and critically appraise multivariable prediction models for the future occurrence of frailty in people living with HIV and to assess and summarize their methodological quality and predictive performance. We searched PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, Cochrane Library, ProQuest, and Chinese databases (SinoMed, CNKI, Wanfang, VIP) from inception to July 24, 2026. Studies that developed or validated any multivariable statistical or machine-learning prediction model for frailty in people living with HIV were eligible. Title and abstract screening, full-text evaluation, data extraction (Checklist for Critical Appraisal and Data Extraction for Systematic Reviews of Prediction Modeling Studies [CHARMS]), and risk-of-bias and applicability assessment (Prediction Model Risk of Bias Assessment Tool [PROBAST]) were conducted independently in duplicate. The search identified 2523 records (initial search: 2205; updated search: 318); 137 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility, and only 1 study met all inclusion criteria. Frail RISC-HIV (Frailty Risk in the Short-Term for Care of People with HIV) was developed in the Centers for AIDS Research Network of Integrated Clinical Systems (CNICS) cohort (n=4680; training n=3170; validation n=1510) using Bayesian model averaging and LASSO (least absolute shrinkage and selection operator) regression combined with Cox proportional-hazards models to predict incident frailty within 2 years. The model comprised 8 predictors (baseline frailty score, depressive symptomatology [Patient Health Questionnaire-7], prescribed antidepressants, current illicit opioid use, current marijuana use, current antiretroviral therapy, age, and sex) and achieved acceptable discrimination in the validation set (Harrell C=0.76, 95% CI 0.73-0.79), with a sensitivity of 80% and specificity of 61% at a 5% risk threshold; calibration under-predicted the observed risk (predicted 7.9% vs observed 14.7% in the validation set). PROBAST assessment rated the study at high overall risk of bias, driven primarily by the analysis domain. To our knowledge, no external validation of the model was identified, and TRIPOD (Transparent Reporting of a Multivariable Prediction Model for Individual Prognosis or Diagnosis) reporting was incomplete. Quantitative synthesis was not feasible. The evidence base for frailty prediction in people living with HIV currently comprises a single, internally validated model that has not yet been externally validated. This critical evidence gap underscores an urgent need for further model development and rigorous external validation in diverse settings, with standardized frailty definitions and reporting in accordance with TRIPOD.

title: Developing and Externally Validating Machine Learning Models to Forecast Short-Term Risk of Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia.
abstract: To develop and externally validate supervised machine learning models using routinely collected ICU electronic health record (EHR) data to predict short-term onset of ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) before clinical diagnosis. Prospective observational cohort study with temporal model development and external validation. ICUs. Mechanically ventilated adults in a prospective observational cohort (Successful Clinical Response In Pneumonia Therapy [SCRIPT]) who underwent bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) for suspected pneumonia and had BAL-confirmed adjudicated VAP or adjudicated non-VAP status (n = 507). External validation in the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care-IV (MIMIC-IV) included mechanically ventilated patients with greater than or equal to 48 hours of continuous invasive ventilation (n = 2681). Additional evaluation was performed in participants from the Inhaled Amikacin vs. Placebo to Prevent Ventilator Associated Pneumonia (AMIKINHAL) randomized trial evaluating inhaled amikacin for VAP prevention, using centrally adjudicated VAP outcomes. None. We extracted 36 day-level clinical features (vital signs, ventilator settings, laboratory values, inflammatory markers, and support devices) from the EHR and trained models to predict VAP within 3, 5, or 7 days before BAL-confirmed diagnosis. Unsupervised clustering identified physiologic states enriched for VAP-labeled days. In internal testing, the best performance reached an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.866 for predicting VAP within 7 days and 0.843 for predicting VAP within 5 days. Predicted risk increased over the days preceding VAP among patients who developed VAP, while remaining low among non-VAP patients. On external validation in MIMIC-IV, the best model achieved an AUROC of 0.817 for predicting VAP within 5 days. Performance was poor in AMIKINHAL, where only nine of 36 features were available. Across models, influential predictors included ventilator duration and mechanics (e.g., positive end-expiratory pressure), platelet count, and inflammatory markers. Machine learning models trained on day-level structured ICU data with BAL-confirmed adjudicated labels predicted VAP up to 7 days before clinical diagnosis with strong discrimination and generalized to an external health system when key features were available, supporting future prospective real-time evaluation.

title: The Potential Role of Aflatoxin-B1 in Breast Cancer Pathogenesis: Mechanistic Insights.
abstract: Aflatoxin B1 (AFB1), a highly toxic foodborne mycotoxin, has progressively been linked to serious, life-threatening health complications like cancer, particularly in the liver. According to the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), AFB1 and its hydroxylated metabolite, aflatoxin M1, are classified as Group 1 and 2B human carcinogens, respectively. This IARC classification is attributed to the established link between AFB1 and hepatocellular carcinoma. Thus, the potential role of AFB1 in mammary carcinogenesis remains a mechanistically plausible hypothesis supported by preclinical laboratory models. This review integrates and synthesizes the findings from experimental and computational studies to elucidate the mechanisms linking AFB1 to mammary carcinogenesis. Overall, AFB1 contributes to breast cancer through interconnected genetic and metabolic mechanisms involving tumor-suppressing, oncogenic, cell-cycle, and apoptotic genes, regulating cancer pathways. Integrative transcriptomic and machine learning approaches have further identified potential mechanistic mediators and biomarkers. Nevertheless, neither malignant transformation nor a higher incidence of human breast cancer is established by these endpoints. Building on this framework, future research should clarify AFB1's role in breast cancer, prioritize prospective human studies, and inform targeted therapeutic or preventive strategies.

title: Systematic Review of Algal Toxins in Seals and Sea Lions: Could Unexplained Caspian Seal Mortalities Be Related to Harmful Algae?
abstract: Harmful algal blooms (HABs) produce potent neurotoxins, such as domoic acid (DA) and saxitoxin (STX), which negatively impact marine mammal health. To contextualize these threats within specific regional ecosystems, we conducted a comprehensive meta-analysis of algal toxin concentrations in stranded and non-stranded seals and sea lions reported between 1990 and 2025. Following a systematic screening of 2377 records, 15 studies met the criteria for inclusion in our systematic review and quantitative analysis. Both toxins displayed substantial variability among studies. Notably, the concentrations of DA found in feces were markedly higher than in other matrices, and feces appears to be a high-yield matrix for detecting recent exposure. Urine and serum showed moderate DA levels, while fetal fluids were among the lowest. Geographically, most studies originated from California and the Alaskan Arctic. Multi-matrix monitoring of algal toxins is required in remote or logistically challenging regions. We propose that exposure to algal and cyanobacterial neurotoxins is a testable contributor to recurrent, unexplained mass mortality events among Caspian seals (Pusa caspica) and that targeted toxicological screening within the Caspian Sea ecosystem is urgently needed.
